utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. How are you, Mr. Atlija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Excellencies -- good afternoon, Excellencies. Good afternoon to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Atlija.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We broke off when discussing the teacher, so I did not manage to get a satisfactory answer as to what was happening in Brisevo and what the authorities were not supposed to know about; however, if you don't have an answer to that, I would like to ask you why you did not mention him in your first statements. You said that only two Serb women lived there with you, but you did not mention him, you mentioned him only later.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned him later because he worked at Brisevo. He had an apartment in Prijedor and a house in the village of Donji Rasavci. From time to time he came to the house of his wife's father, because he married a woman from Brisevo as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statements in the Brdjanin case, 11962 and otherwise, you said that inter-ethnic life was almost idyllic out there. How can you explain that? How can you explain why you were spying on one another when it was so idyllic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask Mr. Karadzic not to misstate the evidence. The witness didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Correct. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, while I'm on the feet: Mr. Karadzic said, I don't know why you don't mention him in your first statements, and it was in the plural. The witness had only given one statement prior to the statement that Mr. Karadzic took him to on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Mr. Atlija made a statement in Croatia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please help me with that. What was the name, HIC? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave my first statement at the Croatian Information Centre. That's what that institution was called at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you gave a statement to this Court or, rather, this Office of the Prosecutor; right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave my second statement to the commission of the US Department of State. The commission for war crimes. That also happened in Croatia. And at some point in 2000, I believe, I gave a statement to this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So a total of three statements before your first testimony; right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement from the Croatian Information Centre was translated into English and used as a basis for the statement I gave to this Tribunal in 2000; whereas the one that I gave to the commission of the US Department of State is something I've never seen since.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 11 of this statement to the Croatian Information Centre, you said that inter-ethnic relations between Serbs and Croats were absolutely fine and that you played football together, and so on and so forth; however, you were asked in the Brdjanin case how come, when villages, Serb, Croat, and Muslim ones, were practically pure, all of them. And you said, Well, we socialised. So your good relations consisted of socialising; right? Otherwise you all lived in your own respective villages; right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that the villages were almost 100 per cent populated by either Serbs or Croats or Muslims. However, until the beginning of these election campaigns and all of these changes in 1990, there weren't any incidents. There weren't any serious incidents. There weren't any major quarrels or disagreements. We played football together. For example, we played music at parties in neighbouring Serb-populated and Muslim-populated villages. We never paid any attention to what their ethnic background was and what their religious affiliation was. We thought that it didn't matter to them either. Certainly it did not matter to us. The first incidents -- actually, what happened was that you could see that people were not as close as they used to be, when these national parties, or whatever they are called, were being established during the election campaigns. And now, what you said about this spying on one another, I never said that. I never said that there was spying on one another. I said in that statement -- or, rather, I wrote in that statement that this teacher - I don't know what the verb I used in the statement was - now, was it "spy"? - but I did not say that it was mutual. I did not say it was both ways, that somebody was spying on us and that we were spying on someone else and that it went that way. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let us try to get the right order, what the sequence of events was. Do you agree that it was in 1989 that the HDZ was founded in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when it was established in Croatia. I'm here to testify about what happened in Prijedor and in the Prijedor area where I took part, where I felt this on my very own skin. I can say now that I assume that that was the year when the HDZ was established in Croatia, but I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, how far away is the Croatian border from Prijedor as the crow flies?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but it's not far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the HDZ in Croatia won the election on the 20th of April, 1990?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HDZ won the elections in Croatia in April 1990 as far as I know, or, rather, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that before that the HDZ had entered Bosnia-Herzegovina triumphantly, the Croat areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that even the Bosnian Croats voted in those elections in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I cannot say because I was not there, simply. However, that was not the case in our area. There was no HDZ, there wasn't any vote in any election in Croatia, at least not we, the Croats of our area. I cannot say anything about other areas because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wasn't in Western Herzegovina either, but it was in the media. There were these impressive photographs of HDZ rallies with all the insignia from Croatia, with all of President Tudjman's rhetoric; don't you remember all of that?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that there were HDZ rallies, especially in Western Herzegovina. There were such rallies in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina too, but I cannot tell you exactly which month or which year. I can also tell you with certainty that there weren't any rallies that were organised in the area where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How powerful was the Serb democratic party on the 20th of April, 1990, when the HDZ won in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not qualified to answer that question. I don't know how powerful the Serb Democratic Party was, and I don't know in what sense you mean this, "powerful."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you say that before ethnic relations deteriorated in Prijedor things were fine but then the political parties were established. And can I tell you that the SDA and the HDZ had already been established when the SDS was established. The HDZ was established even a year and a half before in Croatia. So who do you ascribe this to: to the SDS, or these other parties that were the first to be established, that actually set the temperature, if you will, in terms of the campaign?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat this once again. I testify here about what happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina; whereas you keep talking to me about when the HDZ was established in Croatia and you compare it to the establishment of the SDS in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Whereas I am here to speak about what I know had happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I kindly ask you not to confuse what happened in Croatia and what happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm not competent to answer questions about Croatia. I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, does that mean that you are going to testify only about what you saw yourself personally?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement, the one that I gave to this Court and the statement I gave to the Croatian Information Centre, I tried to emphasise what it was that I personally experienced, what it was that I personally saw, and what, on the other hand, I heard from persons who experienced this themselves. I always tried to make a distinction in order to avoid any misunderstandings. Also, as far as the media is concerned, now you're asking me about different things from Croatia and you're asking me about the establishment of the HDZ in Croatia and the victory of the HDZ in Croatia and so on and so forth, of course we could all see and hear this in the media; however, as for the events that took place in Croatia, I cannot testify about that. Once again I say, I was in Brisevo, I was in the Prijedor region. I can testify about that, as I've already said. I can tell you exactly what it was that I experienced, what I saw, and what others told me. For example, my mother, who was also there. Also my sister, my relatives, my friends. Whereas what happened in Croatia was quite far away, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 01905236 is the page where you promised that you would clearly make a distinction between what you saw yourself and heard yourself and what, on the other hand, you heard about from others. However, I'm asking you whether what happened in Croatia reverberated in Bosnia-Herzegovina; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again you're putting a question that can have a whole lot of answers. That is an assumption. I assume that all of these events reverberate in Bosnia-Herzegovina; however, I can also tell you that what happens in America or in Bangladesh or China also reverberate in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The same kind of reverberation?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not the same intensity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, let's come to your question. Your time is limited, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this was the question: You pointed out in the Stakic trial on the 3rd of July, 5551 to page 5553, you said that Serbs in March 1992 were in their own cafes or were returning from the front line and you said: [In English] "They used to say they would never allow that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina become Croatian." [Interpretation] Was that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina ever a part of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that these persons who were returning from the Croatian front line were saying this. They were boasting about what they did in Croatia. They said that they would plant onions at the Maksimir football stadium in Zagreb, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you. I'm asking you whether Prijedor was part of Croatia, and was that during the Second World War, during German occupation?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know history, Prijedor was officially part of Croatia during the Second World War. But I'm telling you yet again, I'm not here to testify about the Second World War. I was born almost 20 years after the end of the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, but this is your very own sentence, that the Serbs were saying that they would never allow that part of Bosnia to be a part of Croatia. And that is what you said by way of an accusation. You said that that contributed to a worsening of relations, and I'm asking you whether they had any reason for that. Did you hear Dalibor Brozovic say that Croatia would defend itself at the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Dalibor Brozovic said and when he said it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That will do. That will do. Thank you, I just asked you whether you heard about this. Mr. Atlija, you have already shown your partiality here. I'm just putting a simple question to you: You are accusing the Serbs of raising the temperature there, and I'm asking you whether there was any reason for that.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, I'll answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where I lived and where I worked, they had no reason for that. There were no threats, no military threats, or any other threats by other ethnic communities. That is to say, not from the Muslim community, not from the Croat community. The Croat population in that area, if I can remember the census figures correctly, the census that took place immediately before that, there were about 7.000 Croats in the municipality of Prijedor. Compared to the number of Serbs who lived in that municipality, and Muslims as well, that was negligible, that was tiny. So we could not be a threat to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you brought this up, and I'm saying to you now: Before the Second World War, the ratio was even more in favour of the Serbs, but nevertheless the Serbs suffered in Prijedor during the Second World War at the hands of Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the ethnic composition of the population was before the Second World War is something I don't know. I don't have the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Still I'm struggling to understand the relevance of these questions. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, also can Mr. Karadzic please give proper transcript page cites, because I can't find what he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is on page 5553, when the witness asked whether he spoke to any of the Serbs that you knew about why they were carrying arms, and he answered to the effect that here are the explanation that -- the most frequent explanation was that they only wanted to successfully defend Yugoslavia and blah, blah. But taken out of the context, the witness will find it very difficult to follow your question. But most of all, I see the -- I doubt the relevance of these line of questions. Let's please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this line of questioning takes us to the main question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you said that the Serbs took over the power in Prijedor on the 30th of April. Do you know what was the immediate cause for this taking over of power? Or, more specifically, are you aware of the telegrams which were arriving from Sarajevo and concerned the beginning of the attack against the JNA and the Serbs? There were several telegrams, and the last one which was the most explicit arrived on the 29th. Yes or no? If you were not aware, just tell us. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of any telegrams because simply I did not hold any position nor was I in a situation to know whether anyone received any telegrams or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Do you know that there were long negotiations about dividing the municipality into two or three parts?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard from my colleagues I was still working with that some negotiations were being conducted. But as for the details whether that concerned division or the not, that is something I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that Ljubija used to be a municipality?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that at the time when the Serbs took over the power in Prijedor, the Croats, that is to say, the HDZ, took over the power in Ljubija, the HDZ took over the police station? Is this something you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where you have this information from. It's not true what you said. The HDZ or the Croats did not take over the police station or the power in Ljubija at any moment. That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll come to that. So that means you also did not hear how the Crisis Staff in Prijedor advised the minority Serbs to accept these authorities, to be loyal, and to remain quiet? You didn't hear that?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And were you reading your local newspapers, the "Glas" and the "Kozarski Vijesnik"?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Occasionally I read the "Kozarski Vjesnik."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Tieger, I forgot to mention that we will continue to sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis today in the absence of Judge Morrison, who will join us tomorrow. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also said that permits were necessary for non-Serbs to move around. Did the Serbs need these passes as well?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether the Serbs needed any passes is something I do not know, but I don't think the Serbs needed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, you said that differently in the Stakic trial. You said that you didn't know. And in the Zupljanin trial you said that they did not need them. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please see 65 ter 35042. And in that document the ERN number is 0401-0279.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can the witness be allowed the opportunity to answer Mr. Karadzic's question if he wishes to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, whether -- I'm not sure whether the witness answered the last question. Do you remember that? Did you say differently in the Stakic trial that you didn't know, and in the Zupljanin trial you said that they did not need them? Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can remember, and I'll tell you why I said so. In the first instance I said that I was not sure, and I repeat it now that I'm not sure, but I think they did not need them, because I heard from Serbs later on various answers to this question. If they were armed and uniformed and were carrying rifles, then they didn't need any passes. And they were almost all armed and uniformed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that in the year 2000 in the Stakic trial, and it is on page 5659. However, you actually said you didn't know. And in the Zupljanin case, in 16082, you said that they didn't need passes. Please have a look at this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please zoom in. I don't think that we have the appropriate translation and I don't think that this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, these are Croatian intercepts. The Croatian secret service was listening. And please have a look at the last sentence, which says: "Major Raskovic is the head of the press centre and Major Celjenac threatened that he would have him shot if he did not write and say what he told me and if he went around without any documents." So can you see that it was very strict and that Serbs also had to carry documents on them.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was never presented to me. I never saw anything like this. This is the first time I see it. But let me repeat once again: If the locals from Ljubija who were Serbs travelled to Prijedor, no passes were requested. They would just board the bus and travel to Prijedor. And for us non-Serbs it was not like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How come that in 2002 you didn't know that and in 2010 and 2011 you do? How come that your memory is fresher now than it was in 2002?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My memory is always fresh, Mr. Karadzic, as much as it can be. And if I didn't know something, I always said that I didn't know or that I wasn't sure. But please allow me, I also talk to people. I sometimes have a chance to collect a piece of information or two so that if sometimes I'm not certain about something, I may be certain about that in future. I may find the right answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please now tell us which Serb told you that Serbs did not need any passes?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never explicitly asked, for example, Mr. Zoran Pejic, a Serb from Ljubija, Do you need a pass in order to travel to Prijedor? But I will tell you now that I'm not sure how many times, 10 or 20 or more, I was present when, for example, Mr. Zoran Pejic, or a Serb whose nickname was Steven, I don't remember his name, or Rade Zekanovic, for example, or let me not try to remember all the names, when they travelled to Prijedor, they would simple board the bus and go to Prijedor. They went wherever they liked or they would just go into their car and drive wherever they wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you know they weren't carrying a pass in their pocket?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not inspect their pockets. But if someone who was not a Serb wanted to travel to Prijedor or somewhere at the time, it was a procedure that took hours. You couldn't simply come to the bus station, board the bus, and travel somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll bring another witness to testify about that, as you not know what they were carrying in their pockets. So you had a chance to see the incident in Hambarine. Is it correct that the war in Bosnia began, let me not say on the 3rd of March when the Croatian forces attacked Brod or when they attacked Kupres on the 3rd of April, but could we say that the war began on the 6th of April in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said anywhere that I saw the incident in Hambarine. I emphasised that I heard about the incident in Hambarine. And secondly, the answer to the second part of your question: I think that the war in Bosnia began when the Serbian military and paramilitary formations razed to the ground the village of Ravno in Eastern Herzegovina. I don't know what the date of that incident was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-ha. So that was while Croatia was still in Yugoslavia, so it was a conflict with the Yugoslav People's Army; correct? In 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have told you that unfortunately I do not know the date so I cannot give you the correct answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. So I shouldn't ask you anything about Hambarine; right? You did not see that; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may ask me whatever you like, but I emphasised in my statement that I did not see the incident at Hambarine but that I heard about it. Let me repeat again: I emphasise that if you have read my statement, the statement never says in any place that I saw personally this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It took place on the 22nd of May; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it took place in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that there was an ultimatum by the police that the murders of the reservists should surrender themselves? They included Aziz Aliskovic, who was a policeman. Had you heard that this ultimatum had been issued first and that the dead-line was moved several times?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ultimatum was broadcast on the then-Radio Prijedor. However, I do not agree with your formulation, who were the murderers, or whatever you call them, as I do not know. And I stressed that in my statement. I just know what I heard about the incident, that there was a shootout at the checkpoint in Hambarine, that some people were injured. I even think that no one was killed, but I'm not sure. This time I really cannot tell you whether anyone was killed and on what side. I heard the ultimatum on the radio because it was broadcast all the time, and they wanted Aziz Aliskovic in the first place. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I tell you that there were six lads in a car - two Croats and four Serbs - and that two Serbs were dead, two were seriously wounded, and two were slightly wounded, so of the six people everyone was hit, as I told you, does that sound familiar?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you, I heard about the shootout, I heard about the incident, I heard that there were injured people. I don't know if anyone was dead. I'm not happy to hear that someone was, if someone was, but I cannot tell you anything more with certainty because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you say, because you do say that you saw the attack, you say, "I saw the attack from a tall tree together with Milan Buzuk," and you say that you heard about the ultimatum and so on. Didn't you put it that way in your statement given to the OTP on page 5/6 on the 20th of October, 2000?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, when I said that we were watching the attack on Hambarine, that was something else. That was the attack which followed after the ultimatum. We were on a hill-top, that is correct, we were on a hill-top and we climbed a tree so that we would see better. Brisevo is at an attitude of around 495 metres, almost 500 metres. These are the highest hills and you can see well Prijedor and the surrounding area from these hills. So that we could see the attack on Hambarine well in part. But this is not about the incident. You are trying to represent that I said somewhere that I saw directly the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I said the attack on Hambarine. And how far is Brisevo from Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the crow flies, it's a couple of kilometres. If you drive along the road through the hills and valleys, then it's more. It's perhaps about ten kilometres or so. But as the crow flies, it's just a couple of kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you mean two, three, four?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think around two or three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You then said that they shot at the Serbs as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that one could hear shooting from the direction of Hambarine at the soldiers who were attacking Hambarine. It was just infantry weapons, not heavy weapons, but one could hear the shooting; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the men who were in Hambarine, did they have a choice? Were they asked to surrender their weapons and for Aliskovic to surrender himself, and did they have a choice or did they decide to turn Hambarine into a battle-field?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the Serb side decided to turn Hambarine into a battle-field, and this incident was a good excuse for the beginning. If they only wanted Aziz Aliskovic and a couple of murderers, as you say, it could have been resolved in another way, rather than razing a village to the ground, killing many people, and just driving away many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that. And what you are saying is not true. Something else is true. And please answer my questions. I'm asking you this: whether they had any choice. And let us move on to Kozarac. Did Kozarac have a choice? Was an ultimatum issued to Kozarac to surrender their weapons, and was it only after that that an attack occurred? You also talked about that.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for an ultimatum for Kozarac, I didn't talk about that because I don't know that. And I talked about the attack on Kozarac because you can see it also, but the distance is much greater than the one to Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if you would allow me: As for your question whether they had any choice and whether a condition was set that they should surrender their weapons, why would the Serbs have the right to put conditions to others to surrender their weapons or do anything else or they would be forced to do that? Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, because they were killing soldiers and civilians because they wanted war. Is it clear to you that they were not attacked up until the end of May? If it was the goal of the Serbs to attack them, they could have attacked them on the 6th of April. Why didn't they attack them? So let's leave that aside.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we could also say the Serbs could have attacked them on the 1st of October, the 23rd of November. It's no answer, it's no reason for an attack. Whether they attacked them in May or in April or in June, I don't see any sense in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. It's a sophism, so let's leave that aside. Were aware of the strength of the 5th Kozara Brigade?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war I was, myself, a reservist of the 5th Kozarac Brigade so I knew what the numerical strength in the organisation and the composition of the brigade was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you respond to the -- when you were called for mobilisation from the brigade, in June, I think?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not respond to these call-ups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the fighting for Kozarac lasted between seven and eight days? You spoke about that in the Stakic case on 5558 to 5559, pages of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were able to see from Brisevo what was generally going on in Kozarac, that there was shooting, that houses were burning. We were able to see, yes, that it went on for about seven, eight days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What the witness actually said was: "We could see houses burning and this went on for days, I think seven or eight days." In the Stakic transcript at page 5558 to 5559.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have a look at 65 ter 18474.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know whether there were any armed units in Ljubija, non-Serb paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there were any non-Serb paramilitary units in Ljubija. The only military or paramilitary unit I knew existed in Ljubija was under the command of Slobodan and Djoko Taranjac, who were brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at this document, please, dated 18 May 1992. It says: "In the local communes of Ljubija and Donja Ljubija, a unit the size of a platoon armed mostly with rifles and sniper rifles, in the area of Rizmanovici, Hambarine, and Biscani, there's a unit the size of a company armed with rifles, mortars, and recoilless guns. In Carakovo, a unit the size of a platoon armed mostly with rifles." So do you see that before all these incidents armed units existed in these local communes?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first see this document now on display, written by the chief of public security Drljaca, if I can recognise the signature. But at that time I did not see these reports and I did not know anything about this at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1816, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that on 27 May the first attack on Brisevo occurred, and it was a Croat, Nikola Juric, who was behind that attack.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that Mr. Nikola Juric was behind any attack. I'm asking you again not to put words in my mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says, statement to the Croatian Information Centre made in January 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D04471.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say, on page 7: [In English] "... a delegation of men from Brisevo went to Rasavci and to ask why they were being attacked. The Serbs told them it was a warning and that they should surrender all weapons, especially Bofors. The person behind all these was a Croat called Nikola Juric."

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said Nikola Juric was behind the attack. The attack was not organised or led by Nikola Juric. And as far as we were able to learn later, Nikola Juric deliberately provided wrong information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean to the Serbs? The Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many Croats joined the Serbs in suppressing this armed insurgency?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of armed insurgency you're asking. Just now you asked me about the attack on Brisevo and now you're talking about the suppression of an armed insurgency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's call it crisis. This crises from end May to end July, how many Croats were part of the Serb forces and part of the Serb administration and the Serb leadership? How many Croats wanted to avoid war and join the Serbs in these efforts? Some of them, by the way, called them traitors in public; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you're talking about a crisis. What happened in Brisevo was not a crisis. It was terror against civilian population. It was killing and massacres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's up to the Trial Chamber to decide that at the end. I'm asking you for now: Do you know that many Croats took the side of the Serbs, such as this man Juric who you say provided wrong information to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true that many Croats were on the Serb side. There were very few. What you're saying about large number of Serbs -- of Croats is not true. A few of them responded to your mobilisation call-ups, went to war in Croatia, and took part in these events in the area of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you said you had no weapons at first and then you said you had ten to 11 hunting rifles, plus one to two pistols? You said that in your statement to the OTP in 2000, pages 6 and 7. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that at the time when the Serb units attacked Brisevo we had no weapons because the weapons had been returned before that. Those were the weapons of the former Territorial Defence, several M-48 rifles and some hunting weapons that were properly licensed and in legal possession of the people and a couple of pistols. But all that had been surrendered to the then-Serb authorities or para-authorities. And the attack happened after the weapons were returned. Only when the Serb forces were absolutely sure that there's not a single rifle, not a single pistol, not a single bullet in our village, that's when we were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll see about that now. In another case, at the Croatian Information Centre on the 30th of January, 1D04471, you said that you had the following: five M-48 rifle, one M-47 automatic rifle, one M-48 that you had obtained at the black-market --

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unlicensed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- five pistols and, whatchamacallthem, carbines; right? You varied your statements.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not vary my statements. I'll say it once again. All those weapons had been returned before the attack. All the M-48s, five rifles, one Russian automatic rifle, et cetera, they were returned to the Taranjac brothers who led the Serb authorities then, and the hunting rifles and pistols that were properly licensed were handed in in May after that mortar attack. They were handed in to the Serb authorities in Rasavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that first attack was a warning. In fact, you say this: "There was no damage done."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Mr. Atlija, yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd simply ask Mr. Karadzic not to misquote the witness's evidence. In his statement he says the village had ... and then lists a number of weapons, and then says they were all returned. They were handed over. And that's on page 7 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm just saying that he said they had that many weapons. I don't have the whole statement before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you say there was no damage done after that first shelling?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no damage to property and nobody was hurt, fortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on you say that they asked you to return the Bofors and you said whoever is found to have weapons will go to jail; right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe what I said is this: The Serbian military authorities from Rasavci sent us a message asking for these Bofor s that we never had. And then they said they would come to our village, and with one of the locals they will go door to door searching houses, and whoever is found to have a weapon in the house will be taken to jail and his house burned down. There was no talk about the Bofors anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Still you said that to the -- in the statement to the Croatian Information Centre, 04471, and on page 7 you said the owner of whatever weapon is found would be taken to jail. But as time passes, you intensify your accusations against the Serbs, Mr. Atlija, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. I'm not adding to any accusations against the Serbs. I'm not accusing anyone in general when I'm talking about this attack on Brisevo. I mean the Serbian authorities and the Serb paramilitaries who organised this, but I'm not accusing the Serbs as a whole. I never accuse anyone as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In 1993 you say the owner of whatever weapon is found will go to jail and now you say they would be killed. How come your memory has changed so much?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993 I had no opportunity of saying anything to anyone. You probably misquoted. You misquoted probably by accident. But I don't have the statement before me now, and I can't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of January, 1993, did you give a statement to the Croatian Information Centre?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. You're right. I made a slip, not you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you did speak to someone in 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. I thought the date was wrong, but it's not. You are right. It was on the 30th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you skipped some time and go straight on to 24th of June. But let's go back a little. Do you remember the 30th of April , who attacked Prijedor? Do you know about that attack and who was attacking?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 30th April, you mean 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, 30th of May.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 30th of May, 1992, we were able to hear shooting in Prijedor from Brisevo. Later on, talking to other people we learned more. We were able to hear that a small group of armed men led by Slavko Ecimovic from Carakovo, or Zeger, tried to attack either the whole of Prijedor or to take a part of Prijedor. I can't tell, but they were defeated, captured, and killed. Slavko Ecimovic was taken to Omarska camp and killed there. And after the revenge, his whole family, civilians were killed, his wife, his brother, the brother's wife who was pregnant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see that? Did you see those things you are saying?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer. His children were brought to Rade -- by Rado Zekanovic, a policeman, to Brisevo. All this is very viable, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll ask other witnesses about that. I want you to testify about what you've seen. You did not see on TV the HDZ marching in triumph throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you are telling us about things that you heard about.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then ask me specific questions. I'm telling you what I saw, but you keep trying to get me to give you answers that would suit you. I'm telling you about what I lived through. And if that is not convenient, I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about the 30th of May, the 31st of May, the 1st of June? You don't know about that fighting, or you don't know much. Tell us what you know.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want me to emphasise this, I'll emphasise it. We were able to hear shooting in Prijedor from Brisevo. We were not able to see it because Prijedor is a town not so close to Brisevo, so we can't see what goes on there. But it's true we could hear the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you talk about the next crisis, or attack, as you wish, in Brisevo on the 24th of June, 1992; correct? 24 of June?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brisevo was attacked on the 24th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look, please, at 1D4473.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here's what it looks like seen through the eyes of the military intelligence service, the 6th Partisan Brigade. I believe it's from Sanski Most. Extremists, Muslim extremists are coming; preparations are going on against the Serbian people for conspiracy; groups of extremists are pulling out of populated areas into wooded areas; and they use dugouts, they conduct training there. By night they bring food and other stuff. More numerous groups are in Kurevo forest. Around 100 Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have a reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Brisevo, up to 15; in Carakovo, up to 30 extremists. And in the wider area of Stara Rijeka mine, about 50 extremists, Green Berets. And it says, Block enemy forces in certain places, including Atlija village. Block the enemy forces and prevent them from withdrawing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The units should be given combat sets. Support to be given by a mortar platoon 120 millimetres from Javorik area. Prepare them for firing on Brisevo and Kurevo. Number 9, it is strictly prohibited to open fire unless necessary, that is, until the enemy appears. This is Colonel Basara who was rather well spoken about in this courtroom even. Are you deceiving me, Mr. Atlija, or did you not know about the existence of such information?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not deceiving anyone, Mr. Karadzic, least of all this Honourable Court. But I'm more and more inclined to believe that these documents do not tell the truth. They were no military units in Brisevo. I was living there at the time, and I can guarantee there were no military units at the time in Brisevo except when the members of your 5th Krajina and 6th Kozara Brigade arrived. What this says here, it's strictly prohibited to open fire until necessary, what did they consider necessary? Fire was opened against women and children and men. Not a single woman, child, or man was killed in Brisevo carrying weapons or wearing a uniform, so you cannot convince me now that there were any military units in Brisevo that offered resistance to the 6th Krajina and 5th Kozara Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you not say that soldiers came to the village and asked who was firing at them, and you said that no one was firing from there, and they said all right and that there was no reason for you to worry, and they just; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were hiding in the basement, since it was made of concrete, and we were hiding from all the shelling. Soldiers came with insignia. My father and Pero Dimac left the basement, and they were shouting, Why -- they were shouting, Who is firing at us? And my father answered, No one is firing. See, we have no weapons. And they asked, Who is in the basement? And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness start answering again. He is speaking too fast for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, could you repeat your answer again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were hiding in the basement because there was shelling. Ten or 12 soldiers came wearing military police insignia with red bands around their sleeves. My father and Pero Dimac went to the soldiers, and the soldiers were shouting, Why are you firing at us? And my father answered that none of us were firing, that they were the only ones who were shooting, and he said that we have no weapons anyway. They asked him who is in the basement, and his answer was that there were only a few women in the basement. The soldiers said that he could go home, that there was no need for him to go on hiding. Unfortunately he did what they said, and was killed in front of the house.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1817, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, in the neighbouring locations that are referred to here, Carakovo, Kurevo Brdo, Suma, et cetera, were there any [Realtime transcript read in error "my"] military units there, were there any dugouts and trenches or, rather, bunkers? Yes or no or you didn't know? Just say freely whatever you want.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always speak freely. And I'm not saying what I want, I'm saying what I know. We did not know because our movement was highly restricted, and I did not move about these mentioned villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. At that point in time you didn't know that. Did you find out later on? Because many of the things you are testifying about here are things that you found out later on. Did you hear about the infrastructure and the forces in Kurevo later?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of infrastructure you're talking about. But I did know, I heard later on, that from Ljubija this was organised by the Taranjac brothers, or, rather, the unit that they commanded, that a few times they went to carry out the so-called mopping up of Kurevo and then firing could be heard from there. Personally I was not there. I did not go deep into that forest at Kurevo Brdo. I could not see for myself whether there were any dugouts or bunkers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could a correction please be made here on page 28, line 20. It says "my military units." And it is not "my military units." These are not my military units. These are military units that belong to these local communes, Croat and Muslim ones. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now you say that this was restricted for you, and let's see what you said. They came and they were looking for certain people; right? They wanted to see -- they were asking to see -- there was a Croat there, a Croat; right, Baja Bijekic? Among those who had come, there was Dragan Vikic, Radola Dulavic [phoen], Baja Bjegic [phoen], who was also a Croat, and you say that the others were Serbs. And they were looking for Jozo Buzuk, Juro Jakara, Jago Ivandic; is that right? However, they were not there, so they were also looking for Joso Vajicic [phoen], Vinko Mila, Vlado Marasic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They were not at home. These Croats who they were looking for, they were not looking for just any Croats. They were looking for the Croats that you mentioned in this statement; right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you are talking about villagers who were taken to camps. This was before the attack on Brisevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 24th of June, you say that they came and they were looking for certain people; right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. They found some of them at their homes and they picked them up in the van or bus that they came in. As for others, they asked about them in front of the store in Brisevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, they were not at home. And you say that your moment was restrictive; right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Brisevo is 9 square kilometres. So if movement was restricted, that does not mean that everyone just had to be sitting at their homes. They could go to the store or they could go into the fields where people were still involved in agricultural work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also say that some persons were told to report to the police regularly; right? Were you told to report to the police?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some were sent messages to the effect that they should come for an interview. And whoever went never returned. Rado Zekanovic, a policeman, asked Nedo Mlinar, a local person, about me and Emilko Vidakovic; however, I did not report to the police station in Ljubija and neither did Emilko. Fortunately I did not report to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that on the 15th of July there was this quarrel with the soldiers there, and you describe this incident involving a few drunken soldiers; right? Their car broke down and then they asked for help, these Croats came, they offered them brandy, they got drunk, and they quarrelled; right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not right, Mr. Karadzic. These men who came to help, because they were asked to help get the vehicle out, they were offered a drink, they refused, and then they were forced to drink. They were beaten, mistreated, and Milan Ivandic was cut with a screwdriver in the leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on you said -- I have to skip some of these things. So you heard about this incident as well and you did not see anything. Who told you about this incident?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard about it from Milan Ivandic's brothers who were participants. Unfortunately they were all killed later, Milan and his two brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At one point you say that Milan Buzuk said that to you, and in another place you say that it was his brother or your brother who told you about that. Who said that to you exactly?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brother was not there at any point in time. Milan Buzuk was also present. Pejo Ivandic, Stipo Ivandic, Milan Ivandic. Milan Ivandic was stabbed in the leg or foot. Stipo and Pejo, or his brothers, they were present, and Milan Buzuk is a neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This lake, how far away is it from you?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean from the house where I lived?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Brisevo?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A couple of hundred metres is -- from the road that goes from Brisevo to Rasavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in June you went swimming in that lake; right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now we're talking about the lake in Stara Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially it belongs to Stara Rijeka. That is further away, perhaps two and a half kilometres, not only a couple of hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you could go to that lake and swim; it wasn't that your movement was all that restricted?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you think that two or three kilometres of freedom of movement is sufficient for proper living, that is your own view. But from my point of view, that is highly restrictive movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So on the 24th of July in the morning, at what time did this attack start, this July attack against Brisevo?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 3.30 in the morning. That's when the first shells exploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, in the Zupljanin case you said that it was around 4.30. 16095 is the page reference. But that doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you need to think about wrapping up your cross-examination in about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was -- Mr. Karadzic may have misspoke when the question was: "And in June you went swimming in that lake; right?" If he wants to put that -- the month to Mr. Atlija again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was whether in June and July, before ever this attack on the 24th of July, they went swimming. And his answer was that, yes, they did go swimming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I cannot wrap up in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've already answered that you could get to the lake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you did go swimming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: After having spent so much time on marginally important, irrelevant questions, you can't complain about shortage of your time. You have five minutes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I kindly ask that you ask the Prosecution not to put marginal things into their statements. I don't know what marginal is. I don't know what can be a basis for a conviction. Why do they bring in such an ambitious witness who saw one single killing? And that was something that happened when a man was allegedly told to run and he started running and we have lots and lots of information that is hearsay, twice removed. So it's not my problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would put questions instead of making submissions, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue. By the way, you have re-examination, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Not at this stage, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Further on you say that there were Chetniks, there are lots of them. Do you call all Serbs Chetniks or were these really Chetniks that you recognised by something?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't call all Serbs Chetniks. And I said that I do not accuse or condemn an entire people or nation. I do not consider them all to be the same. However, there were quite a few of them with cockades from the Second World War, there were those with insignia of the White Eagles, there were those with crosses with the four Serb Ss, and most of them wore insignia and uniforms of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that you talked to many families of victims; right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Practically all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For what purpose?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, these are people I spent my entire life with. And it was only natural that I wanted to find out and express my condolences. Quite simply to organise ourselves for the future, how to survive, what do we do, how we get out of the area, who was still alive, who was killed, how to bury the dead, which was not easy at all, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you collected this information from them and you included this information in your statements; right? And this indirect information comes from these conversations with families; right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to point out, Mr. Karadzic, what I saw myself and what I stated on the basis of what I found out from conversations with third persons, family members or others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Pero Dimac, you say, was told to run into the forest and then they fired at him. And that's the only killing you saw; right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the only killing I saw. And he was not told to run into the forest. He was told in which direction he should run. He didn't manage to take two steps. They shot him in the back of the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were nearby and you heard what they said to him?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't even 15 metres away from the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you were very afraid of the Serbs if you were only 15 metres away from them; right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not have a choice. I had no opportunity to run further. And, by the way, may I say that I do not fear anyone but God.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you made your statements to groups of your 12 -- 12 of your friends and then you tried to adjust these statements, stream-line them?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We weren't streamlining anything. After giving statements to the Croatia Information Centre, with these 12 or so survivors from Brisevo, we read this statement together once again. Quite simply I wanted to hear their view, I wanted to be as objective as possible, because no matter how objective I tried to be when making a statement, there is bound to be some subjectivity as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You wanted this to be a collective thing? You wanted to be rendered equal, you wanted to inform them and they inform you; right?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not a collective thing. Quite simply I wanted to hear their views. Whenever one reads a statement, one can find things. When we read this transcript afterwards, we will see that there will be typing errors, small errors in the actual wording, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at 2002 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the page reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, look at 1196, what your answer was. I think this is the Stakic case. I'm going to read it out in English so that the interpretation is more correct: [In English] "A great deal of what you said in that statement was based upon what you had been told by other people and not your own personal knowledge; correct? "A. It's true that there are parts that are based on information I received from other people, but in my statements here, I tried to separate what I personally saw and experienced and what I heard from somebody else." [Interpretation] You say that you met with this group, whether they were in Zagreb, these 12 people; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the time we were all in Zagreb. And as I said, and as I said in the Stakic case, I'm trying, when giving statements and when I'm questioned, to emphasise what I heard or saw personally and what I heard from somebody else or learned from another source, and I'm doing it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could give the page number again in the Stakic case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 119 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Transcript page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think Mr. Karadzic is quoting from the Brdjanin case if it starts "119."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, it's from 2002. It's 1D4470, as I have it. And we have it under the "1D" number. Yes, you are right, it's Ackerman. He is the Defence attorney. I apologise, it is Brdjanin. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What page number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It's time for you to come to your last question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What are you talking about, Mr. Karadzic? Brdjanin transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We also have the following page where there is talk about the casualties in Brisevo, where the witness said that a total of 68 persons were killed, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's included in his Stakic transcript. But can Mr. Karadzic just give me the page number of the Brdjanin transcript that he just cited to a moment ago. The interpreters didn't catch the transcript page. He started to say "119" and didn't finish the page number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have it, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 11966. 11967. Page 40, under 1D4470. In e-court it's page 40. 1D4470, if you want a 1D. And the transcript is 11966 and 11967.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no objection from you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. There's no point. Mr. Karadzic just read to the witness what he said in the Brdjanin case. The question and answer were read into the record, so I don't know why he would need these two pages as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I don't see any harm in admitting those two pages to understand the context. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D1818, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, you said that you were present during almost all exhumations. When did these exhumations take place?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they took place in nineteen -- I think that it was the first -- the casualties who were buried in the Grosica [phoen] cemetery, between Midar [phoen] and Stara Rijeka, who were exhumed. And then later the casualties who were buried in the places where they were killed, in fields, forests, and gardens, they were exhumed later on. I don't know exactly, but I think it could have been in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-ha. So the first one took place when?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact year. I can't think of the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you say you saw or somebody told you that traces of teeth could be seen on the breasts of one of the casualties; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct, Mr. Karadzic. That was not during exhumation. That was during the burial of the casualties when they had recently been killed. And I think this was Kaja Komljen who was lying in a field undressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, I will tell you now, because I believe we will need to call you again, there will be reasons for that, you are an activist who interviewed people, collected information, experience of other people, the positions of other people, and then you presented that here in -- on various occasions in the statements which you gave in Croatia and to the Americans and also the statement to the OTP and on the several occasions when you testified. So what you saw was one murder and you do not know whether there were any units there but you interviewed all casualties, witnesses, and you prepare yourself to be a witness activist?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct, Mr. Karadzic. I'm not anyone's activist. I did not do any explicit interviews with anyone. I have other concerns. I have to take care about my life and the life of my own family. And as for the idea that you want to call me again, no problem. Whenever you want me, I will place myself at the disposal of this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that we have exhausted the questioning of this witness, even though I'm an amateur, for me everything that is included in a statement is dangerous for me because I don't know what the Trial Chamber will focus its attention on, so I would kindly ask Mr. Robinson now to say what are the reasons to re-call this witness, and that will be our next motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Ms. Sutherland, you do not have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, before you do excuse the witness, I just have one matter that I wish to bring to the Chamber's attention. I think it can be done in the presence of the witness because I also would be asking you to ask the witness a question about it. You know that we filed our 60th motion for finding of disclosure violation concerning disclosures that were made last week just prior to the commencement of the cross-examination concerning a letter written by the Prosecutor on behalf of seeing that the witness not be repatriated to Bosnia from the country where he was living. Yesterday we received another four documents, and today we have filed a supplement to that motion which attaches the four documents for further consideration by the Trial Chamber. In addition, there's a reference to yet another document which has not yet been provided to us concerning the Prosecution's efforts on behalf of this witness, and so we have decided that in view of, number one, the lack of complete disclosure and, number two, the lack of time, that we would address that issue after the Chamber ruled, either by asking that the witness be re-called or by submitting a motion for admission of those documents through the bar table. So I wanted to make the Chamber aware of those circumstances. Thank you. Excuse me, and the one thing I did -- I want just to ask the witness, if the Chamber would agree, is whether or not the fact of the identity of the country where he is currently residing is something that should be kept confidential or whether he would have no objection to that being made part of the public record. We filed our annexes all under seal at this time just so that the witness could have the option of telling us whether that's a matter he prefers to be confidential, but we would appreciate if the Chamber could find that out from the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And other than that, you do not have any questions to be posed to the witness in -- with respect to that matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I don't think we have the complete information yet that would allow us to put proper questions to the witness on the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Atlija, can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you mean the question about the country in which I reside currently, I can answer that I live in the Federal Republic of Germany.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then that concludes the evidence of yours, Mr. Atlija. On behalf of our Chamber and the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we'll rise all together. We'll take a break and then we are going to hear the evidence of a protected witness. But before that I take it there are some -- several administrative matters to deal with in the absence of the witness. We'll take a break for 25 minutes and resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As indicated, there are a few matters to deal with. First, let us deal with the -- start with a minor issue. It's related to the motion for extension of time to respond to Rule 92 quater motion. Mr. Robinson, could you confirm whether the Defence has now been provided with the 15th of September, 2011, confidential decision in the Tolimir case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we have been provided with that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I take it then you are going to respond 14 days as of today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'd appreciate that. I think we can get it in considerably sooner than that, but to sense a matter of principle, if we can have 14 days from the time we received it, it would be good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It is so ordered. And I -- there's a motion pending with respect to the protective measures for the next witness, but we'll give the -- our ruling when the witness is brought in in private session. Other than that, there's a matter you wish to raise with the -- with respect to the witness after the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't necessarily need to raise it with you. I just wanted to alert you that we filed a written 61st notice of our -- 61st motion for a finding of disclosure violation with respect to that witness, so I don't believe that it's any need to discuss it at this moment. But if you could look at that, and perhaps it can be responded to in the normal course, but we're asking that the witness's testimony be excluded. And that was also the relief that we asked for with this last witness, and you took the motion under advisement. So if you proceed in the same manner, there may be no need for you to re-rule on the motion before the witness is heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I am afraid the Chamber hasn't seen your motion today. Is it related to Mr. Mevludin Sejmenovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, it's a similar issue to that with the last witness. We received just yesterday a disclosure from the Prosecution that it had intervened in his residence situation by writing a letter to a government, and based on that we've asked the Chamber to make a finding that that what a violation of Rule 68 not to have disclosed it to us earlier and asked for remedies, including exclusion of the evidence of the witness and order for further disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was that the only motion that you want -- intended to raise in relation to that witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that you are minded to raise an issue with respect to the way in which the witness should give his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's also correct, and I'm sorry, I completely forgot about that. We are also asking that that witness testify viva voce. And if you like to be -- have me be heard on that now, I'm prepared to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. So you have, as the 92 ter evidence, a 720-page transcript of the witness's testimony in the Stakic case which covers subjects from A to Z.
