You told Dr. Karadzic last week that it's not necessary in his cross-examination for him to rehearse with every witness all of the different aspects to the conflict, and that's exactly what this testimony by the Prosecution does. And we believe that, first of all, the time you allocated for cross-examination based on that scope of 92 ter evidence is very inadequate. It was four days of testimony, and you've given Dr. Karadzic five hours for cross-examination. And we believe that it would be more fair that the Prosecution be required to lead the witness viva voce, since it has not chosen to limit the 92 ter materials, and therefore the proportion of cross-examination that you will allow will be more in line with the topics and the scope of the witness's testimony, and that the Prosecution can then tailor its viva voce examination to those matters which are truly necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I hear the view on this on the Prosecution. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Essentially the position taken by Mr. Robinson is unfounded for a number of reasons. It's factually inaccurate. He doesn't assert a legitimate basis for denying the admissibility of this transcript under 92 ter. And, in fact, the Trial Chamber has dealt with the issue in any event. First, the citation to the number of pages is extremely misleading. As the Court may already be aware and as Mr. Robinson should be aware, the size of the transcript was swelled enormously by the practice in that Chamber of reading out the entirety of every document referred to. And as it happens, the number of subjects covered by this witness, who focuses on the municipality of Prijedor, is no greater than, in fact, is significantly less than that covered by any number, in fact quite a number of other witnesses whose evidence has properly been admitted under 92 ter. Secondly, the breadth, the alleged breadth of a statement is not a basis for denying admissibility under 92 ter, and it presents no reason for doing so. As it happens, the Court has dealt with the alleged breadth of the statement by providing a large number of cross-examination hours to deal with the issues raised. Notwithstanding the fact that there were days and days and days of cross-examination which are fully encompassed in the amalgamated statement. This -- the amalgamated -- not the amalgamated statement, in the 92 ter statement. This was a testimony given before a Chamber in this Tribunal in a single case. It was appropriate in that case, and it's quite appropriate in this case. It would be wholly contrary to the letter and spirit of 92 ter to reject the submission of the entirety of that transcript, including the extremely lengthy cross-examination, without a redaction or reduction on the basis of the representations made by Mr. Robinson, particularly when the Court has allotted quite a number of hours for cross-examination and therefore dealt with any concerns about the alleged breadth of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you referred to the practice of that Chamber. Bearing that in mind, and also given that this witness is purely, if I can say so, a crime-based witness, could you not have produced a succinct statement as an amalgamated statement instead of tendering those 734 pages of lengthy transcript, which we should still read every page of them and summarise them?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The point, Mr. President -- the point on that is, I mean, the documents that are appropriate can be and would be referred to in an amalgamated statement in any event. They would just be referred to, as they typically are, by ERN number. In this case, the length of the statement is increased by the fact that you can, instead of turning to the underlying document, you can see it in the transcript itself. I don't think that that increases the work of the Chamber. Given the -- and given the witness's position, it would have been conceivable and maybe even extremely tempting for the Prosecution in the Stakic case and for the Prosecution producing an amalgamated statement to go into vast detail about the work of the republic assembly, the issues addressed there, the interactions between participants at that level, the objectives expressed by the Bosnian Serbs, and so on, but that is not part of the testimony in the Stakic case, which moves rather rapidly through the back-drop events - once the listing of the documents is excluded - into the events, into the crime-based events. So not surprisingly there are references to what was happening in Prijedor prior to the attack on the Muslim civilian population, including arming of Serbs and so on, but that has never been considered an improper basis for the submission of a 92 ter statement. And it simply -- it's simply not the case that the testimony in the Stakic case represents some lengthy foray into marginal matters. And to suggest that the length of the transcript indicates that is not accurate. And that's what I'm trying to indicate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I tend to agree with the observation that the size of the Rule 92 ter statement itself is not an obstacle for its admission, but you also agree that the -- it is entirely in the discretion of the Trial Chamber whether or not to admit -- or to admit the Rule 92 ter statement; is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I think there are discretionary matters affecting that. I don't think it can be can or should be done arbitrarily. I don't think the Court means to do that. What I'm indicating to the Court is that the Prosecution has abided fully by the letter and spirit of 92 ter in this case. I don't believe that such a motion by Mr. Robinson would have been made if he was as familiar with the transcript as I am from parsing it out. I think it's a reaction to the number of pages. I think that simply means that documents which normally don't consume that -- which normally aren't contained in, but referred to instead, as in this Chamber, we don't read out the entirety of the documents, and anyone following the transcript would be expected then to go to the underlying document. This is -- it is not the case here that the Prosecution has improperly exploited the terms of 92 ter to include material that should not be by the Court and unfairly places a burden on the participants. It is the case that it simple provided the Court with a transcript that was acceptable in another case and that is fully in harmony, in fact, if not lesser in scope than many, many 92 ter statements or packages that have previously been admitted by this Chamber. And that's why I focused on the potentially misleading aspect of the number of pages, because otherwise I think it would be completely apparent that this is a 92 ter submission that is wholly in keeping with the practice of this Chamber and the letter and spirit of 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, if I could just reply briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me put just one question to Mr. Tieger before I give the floor to you, Mr. Robinson. In light of that specific practice before the previous Chamber, how long would it take if the witness is led live for your examination-in-chief? If you can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't think I'm in a position to say, Mr. President, but far -- certainly longer than -- and, I would submit, unfairly longer than is -- than clearly than would be consumed by the 92 ter, the submission, and with a degree of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it would be shorter than five hours which we allocated for the time for the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Mr. President, I would -- I don't -- well, you're asking me to make a representation on -- based on work that I have not yet undertaken. I'm more than satisfied that the five-hour allocation is completely appropriate, in fact, generous, given the inclusion of the lengthy cross-examination in the 92 ter submission. And I'm also fully confident that any practitioner, even one who deems himself to be amateurish, could cover all the issues raised by this 92 ter submission in the five hours allotted, even if he chose to tread over the same ground covered by the previous cross-examination. THE COURT: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, the one thing that I noticed about this transcript in particular, apart from its length, was that it wasn't limited very well to what the witness himself had experienced. Unlike most of the other witnesses that we've had 92 ter statements. There's a lot of discussion about politics, about the background of these events, and I think that distinguishes it, more so than the length, from other examinations that we had. And if we hadn't already heard from Mr. Donia and Mr. Treanor and other witness, perhaps this would be a good witness to ventilate all of those issues with, but my point is that at this stage of the trial, to have all of those issues as part of the direct examination, I think, would be wasteful and unfair given the limitation on the cross-examination time. And finally, with respect to the cross-examination that was done on behalf of Dr. Stakic, Dr. Karadzic hasn't found that to be particularly useful and particularly germane to the issues that he wishes to raise, and it certainly wasn't successful, as Dr. Stakic is serving a very long sentence. So he doesn't feel that he ought to be bound or in any way restricted as a result of that cross-examination that was done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I have to respectfully dispute the accuracy of that submission, Mr. President. There is not, to the contrary, a great deal of time or focus on politics and background. In fact, there's, given the witness's position, probably less than one might expect. And nothing resembling the kind of focus -- I mean, the reference of Dr. Donia is extremely misleading because there's nothing resembling that kind of focus. The witness talks principally about what he observed in Prijedor and not about the general back-drop or context of the issues that may or may not have given rise to the ultimate conflict. And to the extent he comments on politics, it's focused on very concrete, specific events in Prijedor, and moves through them very expeditiously. But if that's Mr. Robinson's problem, if would have been far more appropriate to advise the Prosecution that it -- he -- that the Defence objects to very specific portions, to notify us what those portions were so we could make a determination specifically of whether the representation is accurate and make a determination of whether or not those could or should be properly redacted. This wholesale submission is belated and quite inappropriate and is an attempt to make generalised representations that are inaccurate, in our submission, and translate them into an attack on the entire statement, without giving the Prosecution an opportunity to look at, examine, and dispute, or respond to, the individualized concerns. We continue to stand by our position that this was a quite appropriate submission. It does not contain the broad generalised political discussions that Mr. Robinson seems to be complaining about. But in any event, to focus on that now without notice to us is inappropriate and we should move forward with the -- with the submission. If the Court ultimately determines that the number of hours allocated for cross are -- turn out to be inadequate, given issues that the accused properly or fairly was unable to cover, the Court can respond, but that will, in my submission, not be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have heard -- we have heard the submissions of the parties, and we'll now issue our oral ruling on the accused's request. The Chamber notes the exceptionally voluminous amount of Rule 92 ter evidence sought for admission with this witness, i.e., 734 pages of transcript and 31 associated exhibits covering seven scheduled incidents. As a matter of fact, this led the Chamber to grant five hours of cross-examination to the accused. In light of this submission heard today, the Chamber considers that hearing this witness live is more appropriate in terms of effective trial management. For a purely crime-based witness such as this one, there was no need to present the Chamber with nine days of testimony. This is typically a witness for whom a much shorter statement could and should have been prepared by the Prosecution if it is tendered pursuant to Rule 92 ter. Thus, the Chamber orders that Mr. Mevludin Sejmenovic be heard live, subject to the following decision in relation to the motion referred to by Mr. Robinson. Then shall we bring in the next witness. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, there's one other issue that I notified your staff that I wanted to raise and that is to move to admit a public version or public redacted version of an exhibit that was previously admitted under seal. And I was wondering if this is a convenient time to do that, or I can do that at some other time if you don't want to hear it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could it not be done in writing, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It could be done in writing, but I also would like to read for the public record the portion that was excluded because you ordered that the broadcast be redacted at the time and so it was never actually made part of the public testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But public motion is part of public -- part of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is, but it would be preferable, in our view, to be put in the same position as if we would have been had the document been allowed to be public at the time. But if you feel that it's a waste of time, then I will do it in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Rather than it's a waste of time, but I'm minded more in saving time. So if you could file it in writing, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we need to go into private session in order to bring in the witness? But we need to draw the curtain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, madam. Good afternoon. Before you make the solemn declaration, there is a matter I want to deal with in private session. Could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will now issue its oral ruling on the accused's motion to modify protective measures. Witness KDZ080, filed on 18th of October, 2011, wherein the accused requests that the Chamber rescind the protective measures of pseudonym, image and voice distortion granted to the witness (redacted) because of public statements made by the witness since then. On 25th October, the Prosecution filed its response, attaching a declaration from the Prosecution investigator who met with the witness on 21st of October. The witness informed the investigator that for a number of reasons, including the current political situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, she did not agree to the recision of her protective measures. The Chamber first notes that pursuant to Rule 75(I), it consulted with (redacted) who opined that recision of the protective measures were not warranted in the present circumstances. The Chamber also recalls that under Rule 75(J) the Chamber may order the recision of protective measures, absent the consent of the witness, in exceptional circumstances and "on the basis of a compelling showing of the exigent circumstances or where a miscarriage of justice would otherwise result." The Chamber has carefully examined the Prosecution investigator's declaration, as well as the information contained in Appendix B to the response, and considers that exceptional circumstances have not been shown. On the contrary, in light of the information provided about the increased inter-ethnic tensions in Prijedor over the last few months, the Chamber finds that the continuation of the protective measures of pseudonym, image and voice distortion a warranted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry, but can you move back to private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton, we can safely call the witness "madam witness" or "Ms. Witness"?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back to open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session. Yes, madam witness, could you kindly make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Since I take it that you are well aware of the fact of the protective measures, I will not repeat the explanation. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then could we please have 65 ter number 90289 called up on the screen, please. 90289.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see a document on the computer monitor in front of you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see your name on the document?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is it correctly spelled?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we just have that as a Prosecution exhibit, please, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3690 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And on 21 and 22 October of this year, did representatives of this Tribunal read back to you a statement amalgamating or consolidating parts of that testimony into one document?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I recall that. Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And for the record, that's 65 ter number 90288.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, as a result of hearing that statement read back to you, you identified a number of paragraphs where you wanted to make some corrections; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll read those corrections out to you now, and perhaps you could tell me at the conclusion whether I've covered all the changes you wish to make. First of all, in paragraph 8 you noted that the name "Omer Marjanovic" should instead read "Omer Kerenovic." And in that same paragraph, the name "Sead Mehmedagic" should be changed to read "Esad Mehmedagic." In paragraph 10, to your second answer, "They were taken to Omarska concentration camp and they have not been heard of until this day," you wanted to add: "Their mortal remains were found in mass graves and later buried by their families." In paragraph 27, instead of "and held three fingers crying," that should read "and held three fingers cheering." The last sentence of paragraph 37 should read "they cheered" instead of "they cry out." The last sentence of paragraph 41 should read "war songs" instead of "war cries." At paragraph 46, instead of the name "Said or Sead Burazerovic," it should be "Smail Burazerovic." In paragraph 61, in your first answer, you wish to delete the words "and took us out to shoot us." And in paragraph 79 there was a typographical correction: The word "Zazine," Z-a-z-i-n-e, should actually read "Cazin." Have I covered all the important corrections you identified?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And after noting these corrections on the 22nd of October, you signed that statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With those corrections, are you satisfied the statement that you signed is accurate to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if I was to ask you the same questions that you were asked during the Kvocka and Brdjanin trials, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could then the witness's amalgamated statement 90288 be the next Prosecution exhibit, please, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3691 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll just read a brief summary of that written evidence. The witness is from the town of Prijedor. She will testify about the Serb take-over of the town and the discriminatory measures against non-Serbs which followed, including their forced removal by Serb forces. The witness was then arrested in June 1992 and taken to Omarska camp where she was held until August of that year. She gives evidence of her observations and experiences in the camp and the serious maltreatment of non-Serbs detained there. She speaks of numbers of prisoners being beaten, humiliated, and killed, including persons she recognised. This witness and others would start their day counting the number of dead bodies which had been thrown on the lawn around the "White House." The witness describes the living conditions for women detained at Omarska and how female detainees were physically and sexually assaulted by camp personnel. She talks about the camp personnel, outlining its structure, and gives evidence of a visit to the camp in July of 1992 by a delegation that included Radoslav Brdjanin, Stojan Zupljanin, and others. In August 1992, the witness was transferred to the camp at Trnopolje where she also describes the conditions and situation. In order to ultimately be able to leave Serb-held Prijedor, the witness had to sign a document by which she pledged all her possessions to the autonomous region of the Krajina. And that's the summary of the written evidence, Your Honour. And having concluded that, I'd like to tender those associated exhibits not already entered into evidence, 65 ter 13442 and 13650. Those are the two referred to in the statement which have not already been received as exhibits by Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, those two exhibits will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3692 and P3693 respectively, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I may have to address Your Honour with respect to one of those, that it might be -- need to be under seal, but I'll just have to take a look at the document in the next couple of minutes, if that's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's fine, yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, madam witness, your previous evidence, testimony, has been admitted in the form of a written statement, as you have heard. So now you are -- you will be further examined --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we now in public session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I start with your assertion that you were turned back from work on the 30th of April. Where you work, do guards dismiss people from the kind of position you occupied? In other words, were you dismissed or were you just turned back?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I have described the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] Microphone, microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the witness did not have a microphone on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you not hear the response of the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't understand. Probably the technician can look into the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I think it's been resolved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I start speaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Serbs took over the town. They toppled the legally elected authorities and took control of all important institutions, including the one where I worked. The first working day after that, I went to work as usual, but outside the building there was a group of armed people who asked me where I was going. I said, To work. They produced the list that they had. And when I told them my name and surname, they said I was no longer working there. They did not dismiss me, they just communicated to me that I was not working there any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will try to make my questions as precise as possible, and I would appreciate it if you would give me the briefest possible answers, preferably "yes" or "no." As of what day were you discharged from your position?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I never got an official document from which I could see when I was terminated officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So formally you have not been dismissed to this day?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Well, formally speaking, I did not get it on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that everyone was told during that crisis to go back home for their own safety?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Only non-Serbs. Only citizens of non-Serb ethnicity were turned back from work. The Serbs continued to live and work normally. *Q. You've said that almost all the employees of the court were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: No, I said the Serbs continued to work. Until the take-over, the court was a multi-ethnic institution. And there were, among employees, people of other ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you said that soon after that almost all the employees of the court were of Serb ethnicity. I'm interested in this bit "almost." Who was not?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: After the take-over, persons of Serb ethnicity continued to work in the institution where I had worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said "almost all." I would like to know what goes beyond this "almost."

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you suspected --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have a redaction at lines 2 and 3 on page 63, please. And if we do that, it's okay to leave the question immediately above in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could expand on the reason why lines 2 and 3 should be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's because of the question that was asked: "... you said ... soon after that almost all ... employees of the court were of Serb ethnicity." And in fact, the line of questioning, I'm afraid that the answer which refers to the institution where she worked, it's clear that they're talking about the court, would disclose -- tend to disclose her identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about lines 19 and 20 on previous page?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Actually, yes, apologies. I had overlooked that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then shall we redact the questions themselves?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It would be much simpler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we shouldn't state in this public session that witness worked in the court at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, it's something that would tend to disclose her identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Bear that in mind, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And apologies for not being more precise in my initial answer to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we then please stay on in private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that at this institution where you worked -- you mention a few names, Nedo Ceric, Omer Marijanovic.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Correction: "Kerenovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Keranovic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Kerenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-ha. Sead Mehmedovic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Esad.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Are these names on the same list where your name is when you were suspected of meeting in secret and preparing an armed rebellion? I'm not saying now whether that's correct or not, whether you actually did that. Are these names also on that list?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What list?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, you don't know. You don't know there was this information, this bit of intelligence stating that you were meeting with these people and preparing an armed rebellion?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I do not know this information. That is ridiculous. I met with them even before the Serbs took over. I socialised with them and I worked with them. I was not aware of this accusation because I never received any charges in writing as to why I was detained in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then we are going to deal with all of this not exactly in chronological order. Were you interrogated in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Yes. Just off the cuff, without giving me any sheet of paper, without issuing formal charges, let alone having the right to defence. Nothing was recorded as I was interrogated in the camp. Whatever I said was not recorded. On the basis of this interview with these interrogators or investigators I could assume what it was that I was actually being accused of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What were you questioned about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, madam witness. Do we need to stay in private session?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have to now, now that we're done with the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we go back to open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to put your question again, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What were you questioned about?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Well, if it weren't tragic, it would truly be comical. There were two interrogators, Nenad Babic and Nenad Tomdzic [phoen], that were putting questions to me. For example, one of the questions was whether I voted in the elections in favour of a sovereign independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. *The second question was whether I know Mirza Mujadzic, a man who held a high position, let's put it that way, in the Party of Democratic Action. They asked me whether I met with Nedo Ceric, Omer Kerenovic, and Esad Mehmedovic. These were three colleagues from work that you have mentioned just now. Those were roughly the names that were put.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this will have to be redacted as well now. "My colleagues from work," that needs to be redacted.*

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they ask you where you were staying at the time? Did they ask you about the regularity of the referendum?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I don't remember that they went into that kind of detail. They probably asked me. I don't know. Well, if they knew where I was meeting, they were probably following me. Of course, I stayed at my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-ha, let us see what you said to the expert commission on the 7th of March, 1994. That was on page 3. Let me just see what I have here. 1D04486. On page 3, you said that they asked you about that, whether you were aware of the referendum for independent Bosnia-Herzegovina had been rigged. Did they ask you that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Probably, yes, you've just jogged my memory, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your municipality, who was in charge of declaring referendums and votes, regular or irregular?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: According to the law that was then in force, it was always the president of the court that was the chairman of the elections commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it was the court, then, that had the last say; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: No, not the court. The president of the elections commission. It was the president of the court who was ex officio chairman of the elections commission. It was a commission. It wasn't one man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if somebody would complain, who would have the final say?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I don't know what the second instance was. I really cannot remember anymore. It's been a long time. It was probably some central commission either in Sarajevo or somewhere else. I really wouldn't want to go into that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if it is convenient, the Chamber will take a break now for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume at ten to 6.00. When we resume, madam witness, please bear that in mind for the benefit of having complete interpretation, please put a pause between the question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Talking about the take-over of Prijedor, you said that the non-Serbs were ordered to wear a band around their sleeve; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were the Serbs also wearing bands around their sleeves?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I didn't notice that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 35042, please. Your Honours, is the page which we have shown with the same number acceptable, 0401279 [as interpreted], which was shown to the previous witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's deal with it at a later stage. Why don't we concentrate on this witness now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 0401-0276. Could I now have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to give you an interpretation of a conversation or some radio communication, and all of this was intercepted by the Croatian secret service, they were listening in to all of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We've not been notified on this document, Your Honour. So actually at this point an interpretation of a communication is something I'd object to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is a document that the Prosecution put into the system. But these people in Croatia were not carrying this verbatim. This is the essence, and I can read it out to you, although you can read it yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So on the 30th of May, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There's an objection from the Prosecution, then you should wait for the ruling. There was no notice in relation to the previous witness either, Ms. Edgerton. Are you in the position to answer that question? I checked the notice. I didn't see that 65 ter number. Mr. Robinson can help us, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, I can't, because I'm not involved in that aspect of it. Perhaps I can check for a minute with Dr. Karadzic and our Case Manager. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm informed that there was no notice of either of those two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could tell us the reason why you were not able to notify of this document and then why it is necessary and relevant to use this one with respect to this witness, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, we are dead tired. There isn't enough of us. And I noticed that at the very last moment some kind of racial stigma is suggested. It doesn't have to be admitted, but I just wanted to put this to the witness to show what all of this was like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you said you wanted to tender the part you showed to the previous witness. So it is not your intention to tender this into evidence with respect to this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, but if it cannot be admitted, it doesn't matter. Then I'd just like to show it to the witness. That it's not a question of racism, that it's a practical thing, to mark friends as opposed to foes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber does not see sufficient reason to allow you to put this document to the witness. Move on. Please move on to another topic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I think that's fair, and we're not complaining about that, but I just think it's also an opportune time for me to advise you that we're going to have problems like this in the future. Even as of today we lost one team member because of the reduction in our funding from an issue which has been pending before the president and is not yet resolved. So we have 17 per cent less people to do the job right now that -- and particularly the Case Manager job, which includes translations and uploading exhibits. In addition, we have 150 hours for each employee, and all of us regularly work between 225 and 250 hours per month. So the tasks that are required of us by the Chamber, including giving notice of potential exhibits and submitting documents in advance for translation, are very difficult for us to accomplish. We'll do our best, but that's the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I appreciate your evaluation that our decision was fair and you're not complaining about it. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you said that there was a take-over of power in the municipality of Prijedor. Do you know that what was almost agreed upon before that was to have two municipalities established, a Serb municipality and a Muslim municipality?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Mr. Cehajic went to the left bank of the Sava river and tried to establish a municipality and the police in Ljubija was supposed to be the Muslim MUP?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: This is the first I hear of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what the main reason was for the take-over on the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Have you heard of the 12th of April and then the 17th or 18th of April, but the most important one was the 29th of April, rather, that a telegram arrived on that date from the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of the Interior to start attack against the Serbs and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: This is the first I hear of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then did you hear the Serb side stating what they think they should do and what others should do?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: The local radio was under the control of the Serb government, and the releases were terrible. They were horrifying as far as non-Serbs are concerned. One of them said that the inhabitants of Prijedor who are non-Serbs should put white flags on the windows and terraces of their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that, thank you. This is already May, right? The 30th of May up until the 9th of June. Now, I'm asking you when the Serb side took over in Prijedor, do you remember, do you know? Did they encourage the Muslim and Croat side to establish their own government in their own parts of town?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: No, I've never heard of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At one point you say on the 30th of May Prijedor was attacked. Who was it that attacked Prijedor on the 30th of May?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I heard this. I heard that one group of people that could not reconcile themselves to Prijedor becoming a Serb town and to having Serb iconography all over the place, I'm referring to flags and everything else, allegedly they tried to take Prijedor back to the situation that prevailed before the take-over. I heard about that incursion by this group of people, as you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, so it's a group, not a unit?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: No, a very small group. Too small to oppose the armed Serb paramilitaries and army in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many Serbs were killed then?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I don't know, believe me. You could not believe that radio, that Serb radio, that broadcast information as suited the newly established Serb authorities. Quite simply, the climate that was being created was that all non-Serbs were a threat to the new Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid, madam witness, that it was the Serb people who were under threat and it wasn't the Serb authority that was issuing threats. And the Serbs took over because an attack was being prepared. Let us see what you say in point 13. I think this is from the amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What happened first, madam, the attack or the arrests?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Even before the attack, people who were taken away for questioning. Very often I experienced my apartment being searched, my identity papers checked, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us whether you know that Prijedor was attacked from four or five directions?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the groups, as you call them, reached the centre and that they almost took over the building of the radio, the MUP, and other institutions?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: No, it's impossible that such a small group could take hold of all important places and institutions in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You know, when you talked about that in previous trials, that you were marked as an extremist; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Probably. *Q. Did you read that in the "Kozarski Vjesnik," and did you comment on that in previous trials?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I read it. However, I only read it once I had managed to leave Prijedor. The article that talked about me as an extremist was something I read in the free territory.*

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with me that there were almost 50.000 Muslims in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I do not know the exact figures. I really don't. How many Muslims there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If one-fourth of them were underaged, that leaves 40.000 people, and 20.000 of them would be women. Why were you the one who was singled out as an extremist among them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Well, I wonder, myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that it was an army with various kinds of uniforms and insignia, that they were multicoloured army. What can you say about that? Would you call all Serbs Chetniks or did you really notice somebody who deserved to be labelled "Chetnik"?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I do not call all Serbs Chetniks. I said that among the multiple colours of the uniforms there were uniforms with the Chetnik insignia.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: talked about the bands, and you said that for the non-Serb population it was very difficult, and you said if you wanted to go out to buy something you needed to put a white band on your arm, and on the windows of houses people needed to hang white flags or just white linen. Do you know that it was broadcast on Radio Prijedor that those who would not be fighting and in houses that no one would shoot from they should mark their houses with white linen?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: It wasn't like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that was the broadcast or not?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I don't know that it was formulated like that, with shooting, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Why some Muslims were not suspect at all and some were?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I don't know who made this assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether it was correct that there was a certain number of the Muslims and the Croats who went along well with the Serbs and that the others called them traitors?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Very few. And who dared speak about traitors in the first place at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Maybe they did that later. But would you agree with me that there were many Muslims and Croats who agreed with the Serbian side about the future of Bosnia and Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I don't know. It's possible, but I wouldn't know. *Q. Thank you. All right. Now, please tell us this: The 30th had passed and by the 9th of June -- it was only on the 9th of June when you learned from relatives that the MUP was interested in you and not in him?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And so you reported, and where exactly were you arrested?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: It wasn't a typical arrest. It was precisely my relative who was taken to a concentration camp in Omarska on the previous day, that is to say, on the 8th of June, 1992. When he returned, he called me and said that the then-camp warden and his deputy Zeljko Meakic and Miroslav Kvocka had told him that it was inconvenient, as I had known one of them well, to try and get me arrested in the suburb where I lived, but that I should report to the police station for questioning and that I should report to Ranko Mijic, which I did on the following day. I went to the police station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So he told you that he had been arrested by mistake and that they were looking for you and not for him; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: He told me that they were looking for me. Whether it had been a mistake or not, later on it would turn out that for the newly established Serbian authorities I was, conditionally speaking, more important, and that probably I figured before him in the list for arrests.*

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's why I asked you to identify the areas. But why should this be discussed in private session? Does it reveal her identity?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let me consult with my colleague on that, Your Honour, and be guided by her.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The story of the arrest of her relative on a particular day and the -- his release and advising that she was the one to be arrested, Your Honour, the very fact of that story does go to identify them because it's a unique experience in Prijedor. And, in fact, the brother and sister are easily identified. The difference in their names is only one letter of the alphabet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, point taken. And then that part will be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I cannot hear you well. I hardly can hear you at all.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We also have trouble hearing the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Madam witness, did you hear what Ms. Edgerton said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, unfortunately it was very low, so I couldn't hear well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the unique situation in which the brother and sister were arrested and those lines of question could be revealing your identity, that's what she said, in a crux. So we will discuss it in private session. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And while we're still in private session, my colleagues had time to check the article that Dr. Karadzic is referring to in "Kozarski Vjesnik" and found that this witness is the only woman named among the list of people who were identified as extremists and therefore that also would go to reveal her identity. And that, Your Honour, is at page 73, line 25, to 74, line 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we are still in private session, may I specify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Madam witness, is your brother Nusret Sivac, whereas your name is Nusreta, and the different is only in one name?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: You mean one letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One letter, yes.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that your brother? Were we talking about him?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Let me remind the Chamber that he testified here as KDZ414.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, he didn't have any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. So you came to the police station, but you didn't enter the building; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: That's right. I didn't enter the building. I was standing in front of the entrance to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you were taken to Omarska; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I was taken to the Omarska camp, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for a short while let us remain in private session. Considering your job, you knew how big was the detention unit in the police station?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I was never there. I didn't see how big it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you could order how many people to be detained. Could you order more than ten people?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I never ordered that. I had other duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But would you agree with me that it couldn't have been big?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I really don't know how big it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Namely, you call Omarska a camp. And were there investigation teams who worked -- which worked there daily up until 5.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Investigators came to Omarska every day and they worked from morning till evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that your relative was arrested a little bit after you, maybe a week or so after you, and he was arrested on the basis of the evidence of a man who involved him in his own activity?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I don't know why he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to your knowledge, how many people were staying in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: In Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Omarska, people from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Do you mean the whole municipality? Once again I don't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many people were detained and questioned in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I wouldn't know how many were questioned, but there were thousands of people. Thousands upon thousands, really. But to talk about figures, one has to be very cautious when approaching that. Thousands of people were imprisoned, of all ages, of all professions, all walks of life, including 37 women. There were also underaged persons who were imprisoned at the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the authorities in Prijedor used Omarska as an investigation centre because the detention unit at the public security station is too small?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: No, no, I wouldn't agree with that. That was camp, not any sort of investigation centre. But what is the problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I thought we were still in private session, Your Honour, and I think a large --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, I was about to raise it, whether there's still need to remain in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Go back -- let's go back to open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So my question is this: Do you know that the Prijedor authorities Keraterm, and once it became too small, then Omarska as well, were considered by these authorities as investigation centres which were used for investigations before it would be decided what to do with the detainees?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, in investigation centres people are not tortured, maltreated, and murdered. Investigation centres are something completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have a look at P2772.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Leaving that investigation centre for Trnopolje was on the 3rd of August; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Yes. Departure from the concentration camp Omarska to another concentration camp called Trnopolje took place exactly on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please have a look at this document, which says that 1446 persons were processed, for which valid documentation exists and where there are elements of criminal liability, and that others were transferred to a camp in Trnopolje where there are Muslims who found shelter there, fleeing from the combat operation in the territory of the municipality. The camp is secured by members of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Would you agree with this official report?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I absolutely do not agree. Nothing is true there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that 59 per cent of those who had been detained and questioned were released and 41 per cent were sent to Manjaca and that those who were sent to Manjaca is the number which makes up 41 per cent, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I do not agree with that. I would not go into this analytical assessment of the percentages. Oh, what is it now? I don't hear anything. We have a technical problem. The microphone, it's a problem. It just stops at a certain second it stops, I have no signal, and then again, once again, I have no signal. I absolutely do not hear my own voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I may say, you do not have to hear your own voice. It's better, because it might make you tired, if I can help you.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Thank you for your professional help.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's important that you hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I don't hear interpretation. I absolutely do not hear interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you hear my voice through the head phones?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I hear your voice but again it's stopped. I can't hear you, I can't hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll pause, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear the Judge, yes, I can hear the Judge and the interpreter clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think we are missing any part of your statement so that's -- that may be related to the protective measure of distortion of your voice. So as long as you have no problem in hearing us and hearing Mr. Karadzic's question, we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you answered my question?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Well, I would like to read it, but I'm not sure if I need to. You haven't asked me. I do not agree with this. I said that clearly. I don't agree with your percentages, how many people were questioned, how many were transferred, where. I cannot answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you deny that 1446 persons were sent to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that some people went to Manjaca, but I don't know the exact number. It would be ridiculous if I would try to juggle figures here with you. It would really be something not serious if I were to mention any figures. Some prisoners were sent to Manjaca. This is what I know. And some were sent to the camp in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam, we have information about the numbers which arrived to Manjaca so that the number is indisputable. Can you tell us what was the specific difference, why were you taken in and not somebody else? What was the "differentia specifika [phoen]" for some people to be transferred to Trnopolje and others to be transferred to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I did not determine that. How can I know what the people who decided about the fate of camp inmates used as a criterion? It was destiny that wanted me to survive. *I was the only one who survived from the category of people who were detained at the Omarska camp. Of my colleagues from work who were detained in Omarska, I'm the only survivor from Omarska.*

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come to that if we have time. I'm a little confused by some of these things; once you were outside a SUP building, another time you were outside the court before you were taken away.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I passed by the court to get to the SUP, to the public security station, because the two buildings are close by. And to get to the SUP building, I had to pass by the court building. And I was picked up from outside the public security station before I was taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statements you referred to the legality of institutions of Republika Srpska and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you believe that the referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina was legal, lawful, and that it succeeded in a legal way?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I believe it was legal. It was conducted legally and most of the electorate, the majority of the electorate in Bosnia-Herzegovina voted for living in an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What kind of majority was required?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: If I remember well, because it was a long time ago, 64 per cent of the electorate voted for living in a sovereign independent Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's of move on to other topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me just say that even if that were true, it would be insufficient. Only 64 per cent turned out, and 62, 63 per cent voted. So it was a forcible carving of Bosnia-Herzegovina, forcible possession?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I don't agree with you on that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said - and I'll tell you where - in your statement from 1995, and I'll give you the number in a second. 1D04484. Page 11. You said that at the time court marshals were in place.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: You know what I meant. You find yourself in the camp without any charges brought against you. And whatever you're asked by the interrogators, you have to confirm, you have to agree to. Always under duress and usually with the application of torture and physical abuse. Now, who ordered these executions and this treatment, I don't know. But obviously people had to do it. But when you don't know what you're accused of, what you're tried for, let alone having a chance to defend yourself, and you'd have no idea what they wrote in the minutes because you never get to see it. Whatever -- what are you going to call it except court marshal?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you ever been before the court?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I don't know. The courts were functioning at the time. Why didn't they bring us detainees before the court and try us under law like trials go on in this courtroom here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that there is a preliminary proceeding like here, a preliminary proceeding before the trial, and sometimes the trial doesn't even happen?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Of course not, everywhere, and even in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, you know what the pre-indictment proceedings are like. You have a criminal report, you get to see it, you know what you are being suspected of, you have a right to a defence, you are remanded in custody, you have the right to appeal. All that ceased to exist in Omarska camp. That just did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's be precise. Do you know how prisoners of war are normally treated? Do you have to show them the formal decision to investigate, or do you just capture them and then decide who's a criminal and who's a prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: There are conventions and rules even concerning prisoners of war that govern the treatment of POWs. You don't torture them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We are now looking at the legal side of things. You were not tried for anything or convicted. You were interrogated and released.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I was kept in the concentration camp of Omarska for about two months and then I was taken to another camp, Trnopolje. It's not a remand prison. It's a camp. And I told in previous trials how I lived there, what I lived through, how I was treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Leave that alone. We're looking at the legal side of things.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with anything legal. It's a camp, Mr. Karadzic. Understand that. It's a concentration camp. All the rules are forgotten there. The domestic legislation, international legislation, all that was forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you charged, brought before the court, and is it the case that the longest prison -- longest remand period is six months in our country?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: That has nothing to do with anything. What kind of remand are you talking about? Can you understand that I had no idea why I was detained, I never saw anything in writing. Just watched the torture there. I watched people disappearing. The abuse, the torture. And I was just waiting when they would come --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's stick to my question. I'm asking you: Is the maximum remand in our country six months?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: It was then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You stayed a bit longer than a month in Omarska and five days in Trnopolje; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in books written by people you know Trnopolje is called salvation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: No, it was no salvation to me. I'm speaking from my point of view and from my experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's written in a book that you he must know well.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Everybody has the write to write what they feel, the way they feel. I thought at the time, and I hoped, actually, that perhaps that could be the path to freedom. However, once I arrived there I was afraid over there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Madam, but you stayed there for five days and then you left; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: where?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I corrected that statement. It wasn't on the forehead of this person but on the cheek of that person (redacted) A man walked in there who was not part of the prison staff. When I said "staff," he wasn't a guard. He wasn't the chief. He wasn't among the camp structures, as it were. On that day, a man arrived who wore a uniform and a cap with a cockade and he took a knife out of his boot. He walked up to (redacted) who was sitting in the corner of the restaurant, and he carved a cross in her cheek with that knife. I have already stated this and I remember that scene very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is actually one of the things that we did discuss earlier, Your Honour. If we could go into private session, quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is one statement. A cross on the forehead. *And another statement says -- this is commission of experts, the interviews from 1994. On page 8 you said that it was on the face. However, in "Oslobodjenje," "Oslobodjenje" of the 6th of August, 1997, on page 8, you said that it was on the breast.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: No, no. No way. No way, not on the breast. That is some mistake. On the cheek. On the face.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you correct that in "Oslobodjenje"?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't read that article in "Oslobodjenje." Really, I don't know how that could have been written that way. I haven't read it. This is the first time I hear that that is what was written there, believe me. On the face. Quite clearly. I am stating that very clearly. On the face, on the cheek.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, you said that you remember that very clearly, and now we see that there are three variants.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Well, the cheek is part of the face, isn't it? So there's just one variant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't have time to deal with these discrepancies any longer. But, all right, just a moment, please. When you spoke about the killing of Mehmedalija Sarajlic --

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- you said that you only recognised his body among the others; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He had a light coloured suit that he wore all the time in the camp until he was liquidated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, in your statement given to the commission of experts, you said that you had heard that he had been killed but that you had not seen his body.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I just agree with what I said here before the Court and what is stated in the transcripts from my previous testimonies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This statement that you gave to the commission of American experts, are you withdrawing it altogether?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I don't know. I haven't read it, so I cannot say anything, whether there are any mistakes there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You talk about calls during the night and so on.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: About things that you heard of. However, you did not see these things; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Which things? I don't understand. Would you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Zeljko Meakic, called Jadranka, not to mention her last name, and: [In English] "... all out which eventually became a nightly occurrence." [Interpretation] You say: [In English] "During this period" -- [no interpretation] "... didn't see or hear anything to make her believe that anyone was punished for any of those things to prisoner in camp." [Interpretation] And you say that there were persons who had been killed. Which killing did you see actually?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I saw many killings. I saw many persons being killed, very many. Also tortures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Leave tortures aside now. Which killings?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I cannot remember the first and last names of the persons who were killed, but my day in Omarska started with a counting of these dead people who were thrown out in front of the "White House" on the lawn in front of the "White House."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who can confirm that, madam?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Confirm what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What you're saying now.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: The skeletons from mass graves can confirm that. Do you understand that? Many mass graves were found in which camp inmates from Omarska were found and identified, so this is confirmed by the skeletons, the skeletons of these persons that were found in mass graves. And unfortunately many people have not been found yet, although it's been a long time since.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you describe to us every killing that you saw and what happened?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Well, for the most part --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. You say, on such and such a date, such and such a thing happened. Tell us all of that like a real witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: Oh, like a real one, right? Let me tell you, sometimes a bullet was a gift, a reward, in Omarska. Before killing people, they beat them horribly with various objects.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lady, I really have no time. I would like to listen to all you have. And if you had really lived through all you claim you've lived, I would feel great sympathy. But just tell me, describe a murder that you saw with your own eyes. It happened this and this, this person was ... and then you give us name and surname, and so and so shot him.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: In Omarska people mostly succumbed to the injuries of the awful torture and beatings with iron and wooden objects of all sorts. People were mostly killed by rifle or pistol bullets, but people died for the most part because they couldn't stand this torture. It was not as easy as just taking a gun and killing someone. Before that the person was tortured and abused in all sorts of ways, and succumbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you didn't see a single murder?

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: I've seen many.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Describe one.

utterances.speaker: KDZ080
utterances.text: They torture a man, they beat him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, I'm sorry, but I didn't want to go any further. I'd like to please go into private session and ask for another redaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could the Chamber move into private is session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
